title: Autopsy and Parish
premise: True-crime podcaster Odile Pemberton has built a career on closing cases no one else can, so when she takes on the 1974 disappearance of parish organist Marguerite Voss, she expects a tidy resolution. Instead, the recovered diary keeps writing for three weeks after the date Marguerite vanished, and its final entries describe Odile's own investigation in unnervingly precise detail. As Odile decodes a ledger hidden in the hymnal numbering of Marguerite's sheet music, he uncovers a protection racket run by the town's beloved founding families — and realizes the trial of Marguerite's accused killer, set to begin in six weeks, is built on evidence someone planted. The diary's last entry names Odile as the one who finishes it, forcing him to choose between exposing the truth and protecting the descendant of Marguerite's secret lover, with whom he has fallen in love. In the end, Odile broadcasts the decoded ledger hours before the verdict, collapsing the trial and the town's mythology at once, but the cost is the relationship, his reputation, and any illusion that justice and the law are the same thing.
about_author: E. M. Pemberton is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent eleven years transcribing small-town trials before turning to fiction. They live in a converted church rectory and claim they can still hear the organ.

chapters.title: The Coldest Case on Record
chapters.summary: Odile Pemberton, narrating in first person, introduces her podcast's perfect record and announces the Marguerite Voss case: an organist who vanished in 1974 from a river town that never stopped grieving her. Emotional beat: confident showmanship masking a hunger to matter.

chapters.title: Hymn Number Forty
chapters.summary: Odile interviews elderly choir members; one presses a yellowed hymnal into his hands, insisting Marguerite marked every page wrong. POV shifts briefly to a 1974 letter fragment. Beat: first crack in the official story.

chapters.title: The Diary That Kept Writing
chapters.summary: A Voss family estate sale yields Marguerite's diary. Its final dated entry falls three weeks after her disappearance — and describes a stranger arriving to ask questions about her music. Beat: dread; the case stops being history.

chapters.title: Parish of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Odile moves temporarily to the town, renting a room above the hardware store. Establishes the cast: Sheriff Dane Ashford, archivist Sister Ruth, and quiet bookbinder Tomas Reyes. Beat: uneasy belonging.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Isn't
chapters.summary: Odile cross-references the 'wrong' hymn numbers against dates and finds they form a running tally — payments, or debts. He begins decoding. Beat: the thrill of the hunt returning.

chapters.title: The Accused
chapters.summary: Odile interviews Ray Delacroix, the dying man about to stand trial for Marguerite's murder after new DNA evidence surfaced last year. Ray swears innocence but won't say who did it. Beat: pity tangled with suspicion.

chapters.title: Entry Nineteen
chapters.summary: The diary describes the stranger asking questions — using phrasing identical to Odile's own podcast intro. Odile tells no one. Beat: vertigo; the past watching him.

chapters.title: Sister Ruth's Silence
chapters.summary: The archivist admits the diocese sealed Marguerite's records in 1975 at the request of the Harrow family, town founders. Beat: institutional rot beneath piety.

chapters.title: Tomas Binds Wounds
chapters.summary: Odile brings the fragile diary to bookbinder Tomas for preservation. Their slow-burn connection deepens over tea and marginalia. Beat: tenderness as risk.

chapters.title: The Hymnal Cipher Cracks
chapters.summary: Odile realizes the numbers map to ledger pages hidden in plain sight: the amounts are recorded as verse-and-line citations. First decoded name: E. Harrow. Beat: elation curdling into fear.

chapters.title: Founding Families, Founding Sins
chapters.summary: Research montage: the Harrows ran the mill, the bank, and the sheriff's office for a century. Marguerite was their bookkeeper. Beat: the case widens from murder to machinery.

chapters.title: Someone Reads Over My Shoulder
chapters.summary: Odile's rental is searched; nothing taken but a photocopy of the cipher key. He suspects Sheriff Ashford. Beat: paranoia arrives to stay.

chapters.title: Ray's Confession, Half of It
chapters.summary: Ray admits he burned evidence in 1974 — not of murder, but of the racket — to protect his brother. Beat: complicity everywhere; no clean hands.

chapters.title: The Lover in the Margins
chapters.summary: Diary margins reveal Marguerite loved someone initialled 'C.H.' — a Harrow. Odile finds the line continues: Claire Harrow, now ninety-one, living under another name. Beat: love as the buried engine of everything.

chapters.title: Claire
chapters.summary: Claire Harrow receives Odile warily, denies everything, then quotes a diary line never published. She asks what he wants. Beat: two keepers of secrets recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Duty Calls Both Ways
chapters.summary: Ashford warns Odile off, citing witness tampering before trial. Odile realizes the prosecution's timeline depends on the diary being fake — which means someone needs it discredited. Beat: the law as a weapon aimed at truth.

chapters.title: Entry Thirty-One
chapters.summary: The diary's late entries grow frantic: 'He knows I copied the book. If anything happens, the singing will tell you.' Odile understands the hymns were a dead-drop system. Beat: Marguerite becomes a person, not a puzzle.

chapters.title: The Trial Docket
chapters.summary: Pretrial motions begin; the DA, ambitious and nervous, courts Odile for favorable coverage. Odile plays along while decoding faster. Beat: double game, rising stakes.

chapters.title: Tomas's Grandfather
chapters.summary: Tomas reveals his grandfather was the town's ferryman in 1974 — and the last person to see Marguerite alive besides her killer. Beat: intimacy complicated by inheritance.

chapters.title: The Ferry Receipt
chapters.summary: In the grandfather's effects, Tomas finds a receipt stub dated the night after Marguerite's 'disappearance' — she crossed the river alive. Beat: hope; she may have fled, not died.

chapters.title: Where the Ledger Ends
chapters.summary: Decoded entries stop mid-page in 1975. Either Marguerite stopped paying, or stopped existing. Odile finds a final citation pointing to Psalm 88 — 'the dark.' Beat: grief entering the arithmetic.

chapters.title: Ashford's Inheritance
chapters.summary: Odile discovers Ashford's father was the 1974 sheriff on the Harrow payroll. Confrontation: Ashford doesn't deny it, only says, 'You don't know what she asked us to do.' Beat: the antagonist gains a tragic dimension.

chapters.title: They Know About the Diary
chapters.summary: Someone leaks that Odile possesses 'new evidence'; a motion to seize it is filed. His editor pulls the podcast episode under legal pressure. Beat: isolation; allies thinning.

chapters.title: Night at the Rectory
chapters.summary: Tomas shelters Odile during a break-in scare. They confess feelings neither can afford. Beat: love declared precisely when it becomes dangerous.

chapters.title: Claire's Bargain
chapters.summary: Claire offers Odile the missing ledger pages — if he agrees the broadcast waits until after the trial, sparing her family's last dignity. Beat: temptation of the gentle cover-up.

chapters.title: The Stranger in Entry One
chapters.summary: Rereading, Odile identifies the diary's mysterious post-disappearance visitor: not himself, but a podcaster predecessor who vanished mid-investigation in 1998. Beat: he is walking a worn path.

chapters.title: The Predecessor's Tape
chapters.summary: Odile tracks down the 1998 investigator's storage unit: tapes, half a decode, and a note — 'They let me get exactly far enough to confirm it, then bought me.' Beat: terror of being managed rather than stopped.

chapters.title: Bought, Not Buried
chapters.summary: The predecessor is alive, wealthy, and hollowed out; he begs Odile to take the settlement too. Odile refuses. Beat: the theme crystallizes — survival has a price, and he's choosing not to pay it.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Last Crossing
chapters.summary: Reconstruction chapter, Marguerite's POV, 1974–75: she copied the ledger, planned to flee with Claire, and sent the hymnal ahead as insurance. The boat waited. Beat: full heartbreak of her agency and fear.

chapters.title: Psalm Eighty-Eight
chapters.summary: Odile and Tomas search the flooded quarry chapel referenced by the psalm citation and find a rusted strongbox: the original ledger, and a woman's shoe. Beat: the body — or proof of one — finally surfaces.

chapters.title: Whose Shoe
chapters.summary: Forensics on the shoe match neither Marguerite nor anyone missing — it belonged to the Harrow matriarch, meaning Marguerite took it fleeing and someone else ended up in the water. Beat: the story inverts again.

chapters.title: The Trial Opens
chapters.summary: Ray Delacroix's trial begins amid media frenzy. The prosecution's star evidence unravels under Odile's quietly submitted chain-of-custody questions. Beat: justice stirring outside the courtroom.

chapters.title: Ashford Chooses
chapters.summary: Ashford, confronted with the strongbox contents, makes his choice: he hands Odile his father's old case file and resigns. Beat: redemption purchased with ruin.

chapters.title: Claire Breaks
chapters.summary: Claire, learning Marguerite died trying to reach her, gives Odile the final pages and her testimony. Beat: love outlasting duty, at last, on the record.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Hours before verdict, Odile airs everything: the ledger, the racket, the planted DNA, four generations of names. The trial collapses; the town erupts. Beat: catharsis with sirens.

chapters.title: What Survival Cost
chapters.summary: Fallout: lawsuits, the DA's disgrace, the Harrow name dismantled. The predecessor sends one word — 'Run' — and Odile understands the danger isn't over. Beat: victory shadowed.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: The diary's true final page, unsealed by Claire, names whoever finishes the work — written in 1975, addressed to 'the one who hears the singing.' Odile weeps. Beat: communion across fifty years.

chapters.title: Verdict Without a Trial
chapters.summary: With the trial voided, truth replaces verdict: Ray walks free, the town holds an unofficial reckoning in the church where it all began. Beat: communal mourning and release.

chapters.title: The Singing
chapters.summary: At a memorial service, the choir sings Hymn Forty correctly for the first time. Tomas takes Odile's hand publicly. Beat: grace, earned and imperfect.

chapters.title: Autopsy and Parish
chapters.summary: Epilogue: Odile closes the case file — the only one he'll ever mark 'closed by someone else's courage' — and opens a blank notebook. Final image: the river, carrying what it carries. Beat: peace without absolution.
